newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Weather seen favourable for Russia '97 grain crop.
newsitem.headline: Weather seen favourable for Russia '97 grain crop.

text.p: Growing conditions for Russia's winter grain crop were ideal in many regions this season, and early forecasts for the summer suggest good conditions will continue on the whole, a senior forecaster said on Wednesday.

"Overall we had ideal growing conditions this winter, and so far the spring has been favourable too, with warm weather in March, particularly in the southern growing regions," said Viktor Trenin, head of the State Meteorological Service.
He said that estimates for winter kill losses in 1997 were eight to 10 percent below normal levels, although actual losses would not be known until the end of May.
"For winter wheat the dangerous period can be May, when very high temperatures could be harmful," he told Reuters.
The service's long-term weather forecasts showed that the outlook for the summer was positive.
"In the main agricultural regions -- the European and southern parts of Russia -- conditions this summer are expected to be favourable," Trenin said.
But he added that several risks remained.
In Siberia, where temperatures have been very high during the latter part of March and in early April, cold air over the coming weeks could lead to some crop damage.
Trenin also said that drought could hit some crops in central parts of the country.
"The long term forecasts for this summer show that in the central regions of Russia there could be some drought -- that is in the Urals, in Western Siberia and Central Russia," he said.
Agricultural analysts said it was too early to accurately forecast the 1997 net grain harvest.
Despite a favourable weather outlook, winter sowing last autumn lagged the previous season's levels, they said.
But the early spring sowing campaign was running well ahead of year-ago levels, according to the State Statistics Committee.

The committee said on Wednesday that by April 14, a total of 1.43 million hectares had been sown, 46 percent higher than at the same time last year. Of this total, 941,000 hectares had been sown to grains (excluding maize), up 74 percent.
Earlier this year Russia's Agriculture Ministry said it had targeted net grain production at 70.0 million tonnes, up slightly from 69.3 million tonnes in 1996.

But a document from the Institute of Agricultural Information and Technical-Economic Investigations was quoted by Interfax news agency last month as saying that the net harvest may fall to 63.0 million tonnes this year.
